extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers doing worldbuilding (authors, podcast listeners of Writing Excuses)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writers on designing believable political systems and using governmental structure as dramatic material in fiction. Covers sources of power, enforcement, scale, succession, and techniques for making political intrigue interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start from familiar power structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at the power structures in which you live — family, workplace, personal governance — as the quickest way to make governmental systems interesting and believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the everyday systems around you feel autocratic, democratic, meritocratic, etc.; model fictional institutions on those patterns. This is presented as the fastest way to learn how to make a government feel real in a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define methods of governance (how power is expressed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly decide whether a government is autocratic, democratic, meritocratic, monarchy, etc., and how that affects who holds power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about the methods by which people are governed and how officials got into power (inherited, elected, appointed for skill). Use these choices to shape characters' motivations and conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design enforcement mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how laws and government decisions are enforced — military, police, bureaucratic execution — and how enforcement expresses power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask who carries out judgment and how force is applied. Enforcement mechanisms create opportunities for conflict and drama (e.g., repression, favoritism, breakdowns of control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify lawmaking, interpretation, and enforcement roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide who creates law, who interprets it, and who executes it — the separation (or fusion) of these functions shapes political dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these roles to create checks, tensions, or abuses of power. Consider how crossing between domains (e.g., legislators acting as judges) changes balance and can cause breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the four-estate model as a baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the executive/legislative/judiciary/fourth-estate (press) framework to categorize expressions of power in a society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hosts recommend using that model and then either applying it or intentionally breaking it. Homework: invent your own system along the 'four estates' model or find expressions of power outside it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the source(s) of power and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide where a government's authority comes from (force, tradition, consent, religion, resources) and how its origin affects citizens' attitudes and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical circumstances of founding (e.g., post-gun vs feudal societies) and how that shapes views about government size, scope, and required allegiance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design resource allocation and taxation systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how resources are gathered and distributed — taxes, tribute, resource ownership — and whether a government needs taxes at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about what taxes pay for and how they are collected; a government could instead control a resource or have a direct source of wealth. Taxation creates social friction and story hooks (e.g., Lagaan example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider scale, communication, and administrative capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a government can realistically rule the territory it controls given information and communication constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, governments collapse when they overreach their communication/administration capacities. For large realms, invent plausible delegation, local rulers, or infrastructure (or show why the state fractures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model local governance and plural systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for multiple overlapping levels of governance (village councils, regional authorities, federal/state bodies) and local traditions that can dominate day-to-day life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like the panchayat (five elders) to show how local bodies can wield real power even under larger formal governments; this affects who citizens answer to and where conflicts originate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan succession and transfer of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how leadership changes hands — hereditary primogeniture, election, appointment, emergency selection — and how succession rules create intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Succession is a rich source of drama (e.g., The Lion in Winter, Larry Niven's 'One Face'). Consider mechanisms for ensuring or subverting a chosen heir and the political scheming that follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create focal figures or villains for dramatic clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a recognizable face of the government (dictator, monarch, corrupt official) for audiences to direct emotions toward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not strictly necessary, having a person to vilify simplifies reader engagement with political conflict; democracies often need a public face to make villainy tangible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make intrigue out of navigating rules and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive political drama from how characters operate inside, around, or between institutional rules — favors, quid pro quo, bureaucratic hoops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows like House of Cards, The Thick of It, and Veep succeed by making the struggle to accomplish goals within a system the source of tension; emphasize the 'movement within the rules' rather than only external villainy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the mechanics of power shifts and 'musculature' of politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict the practical actions (alliances, bargains, backstabbing) that change who has power rather than abstract ideology alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think in physical/muscular metaphors (arm bar, rug ripping) — how do people take or lose power? This grounds political conflict in concrete tactics that are engaging to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cultural norms to justify institutional forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Let culture, religion, social norms, and respect structures determine which kinds of government are plausible and how they function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: societies that venerate elders will plausibly use elder councils; North American skepticism toward elders makes that model less believable there. Match institutions to cultural logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for domain-crossing as a corruption/instability signal
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful worldbuilding device is when actors or institutions cross traditional domains of expression (e.g., media acting as judiciary) to create imbalances or corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-domain power (when one actor controls lawmaking, enforcement, and narrative) explains regime failure and provides plot devices showing how governments fracture or centralize power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent alternative expressions of power beyond formal branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek or create categories of power expression outside the standard four estates and build institutions around those unique axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hosts encourage inventing your own numbered model of power (social, economic, ritual, technological, etc.) and using it as the organizing principle for the society.
